phone.inside.title: Layers
captions: A phone is a sandwich of about nine thin layers, all packed into less than a centimetre.
The touch sensor is a grid of electrodes. Your finger changes the electric field, or capacitance, where you touch.
Millions of OLED pixels each make their own light. A black pixel is simply off, which saves power on dark screens.
The logic board holds processor, memory and radio chips. The processor does billions of simple steps per second.
Lithium ions move between two electrode layers as you charge and use the phone. The battery is the largest part inside.
The coil charges without a cable by magnetic induction. The camera stacks several lenses onto a tiny sensor.

phone.flow.title: Follow the energy
captions: The socket gives 230 volts that swing back and forth. The charger turns it into a low, steady voltage.
In the battery, lithium ions are pushed from one electrode layer to the other. That stores the energy.
Using the phone lets the ions flow back. The current drives the processor, the radio and the screen.
In the end all of it leaves as light, radio waves and heat. That is why a busy phone feels warm.

phone.number.title: The number
captions: 4000 milliamp-hours at 3.85 volts is about 15 watt-hours: the energy of one full battery.
Charging it costs under half a cent. A whole year of daily charging is a little over one euro.
A kettle burns through the same energy in 28 seconds. Heating water costs far more than computing.
